html:
The settlement of East Polynesia was the last great human migration into empty land: between roughly 1000 and 1300 CE, Polynesian voyagers found and settled the islands of the eastern Pacific, from the Society Islands to Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa (New Zealand).

The voyagers came from western Polynesia, Samoa and Tonga, where ancestral Polynesian culture had grown from the Lapita settlers. After a pause of more than a thousand years they moved east again, and fast. New radiocarbon dates keep shortening the window: most of the islands seem to have been settled within a few centuries.

How they did it:

  • Large double-hulled canoes, able to carry families, food plants, pigs, dogs and chickens.
  • Wayfinding without instruments: steering by the rising and setting stars, reading ocean swells, watching birds and clouds, all passed down in chant and song.
  • Return voyages, so that people knew where islands lay before settlers set out.

The results are spread across this chart. The moai of Rapa Nui were carved by the easternmost settlers. Hawaiʻi grew into the chiefdoms later united as the Kingdom of Hawaii. The last landfall was Aotearoa, around 1250 to 1300, by the ancestors of the Māori. The sweet potato, a South American plant, reached Polynesia in this period, strong evidence that some voyagers touched the Americas and came back.

Voyaging later declined. Europeans once doubted Polynesians could have done it on purpose, until revived canoe voyages from the 1970s showed that they could.
